title: Expansion and cytotoxicity of mucosal CAR+ T cells in enterocolitis associated with BCMA CAR-T cell therapy - Nature Medicine
byline: Sainz; Tania P; Dong; Sharlene; Mundhada; Aniruddha; Wang; Pleitez; Hector Garcia; Villela; Carla; Henderson; Jared; Ayers; Amy A; Murphy; Karmila; Cortina; Fra
html:
Abstract

Ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel) is a B cell maturation-antigen-targeting chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell product approved for relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma treatment. Previously reported cases of post-cilta-cel immune effector cell enterocolitis (IEC-EC) have been described as a severe diarrhea associated with clonal CAR T cell populations. Here we report nine cases of cilta-cel-associated IEC-EC with CAR T cell-positive (CAR+) infiltration in 158 cilta-cel-treated patients at MD Anderson Cancer Center (incidence of 5.1% at a 6-month landmark and 5.7% globally). Cilta-cel infiltration was the primary cause of IEC-EC, and all cases demonstrated monoclonal or oligoclonal T cell populations as measured by vector integration analysis, flow cytometry and T cell receptor sequencing. Patients with IEC-EC had 100-fold more CAR T cell persistence in the peripheral blood than patients without IEC-EC. RNA sequencing analysis revealed increased cytotoxic and inflammatory programs associated with the CAR+ infiltrates relative to controls. Clonal vector integration occurred in introns of highly expressed genes without evidence of vector-mediated mutagenesis. Candidate driver mutations were sparse and heterogeneous, distinguishing IEC-EC from peripheral T cell lymphoma following CAR T cell therapy. In sum, we find that IEC-EC pathology represents a distinct, duodenum-predominant, clonal lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by the infiltration of clonal CAR+ cytotoxic T cells into the gastrointestinal tract.

Main

Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has led to deep and durable responses for patients with multiple myeloma (MM)1,2. Ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel) is a B cell maturation antigen (BCMA)-directed CAR T cell product currently approved for relapsed/refractory MM treatment. Although cilta-cel is generally well tolerated, it may cause common CAR-related toxicities such as cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune-effector-cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS). In addition to these common post-CAR complications, cilta-cel can cause unique non-ICANS neurologic symptoms, including a hypokinetic syndrome that mimics Parkinson bradykinesia3,4.

Reports of CAR T cell positive (CAR+) T cell neoplasms in patients receiving CAR-T cell therapy have emerged5,6,7,8,9,10, resulting in a boxed warning regarding risk of secondary malignancy after CAR T cell therapies11,12. Despite these concerns, CAR+ neoplasms are still extremely rare. One emerging form of possible CAR+ T cell malignancy described by multiple recent reports is post-CAR peripheral T cell lymphomas (PTCLs)9,13,14, demonstrating the potential for CAR T cells to undergo malignant transformation7,9,10,15,16.

A second form of post-CAR T cell therapy toxicity is immune-effector-cell-associated enterocolitis (IEC-EC). This toxicity occurs in approximately 1–10% (refs. 6,17) of patients treated with the BCMA-directed CAR T cell product cilta-cel and is independently the subject of a recent FDA boxed warning6,12. This syndrome typically causes excessive diarrhea and an inability to maintain an adequate nutritional state. In the small number of deeply characterized cases available, post-cilta-cel IEC-EC closely resembles an indolent T cell lymphoproliferative disorder of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract6,7,8,9,18,19. The largest case series includes 14 cases but lacks comprehensive molecular profiling17. So far, all profiled cases occurred after cilta-cel treatment.

Here we comprehensively profile nine biopsy-proven post-cilta-cel IEC-EC cases. Sequential immunofluorescence (seqIF), peripheral blood flow cytometry, T cell receptor (TCR) profiling, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), whole-exome sequencing (WES), whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) helped define clinical course, treatment, diagnosis and molecular pathogenesis of this disease.

Results

Severe post-cilta-cel enterocolitis is associated with CAR+ T cell infiltration

We analyzed 17 patients among 160 cilta-cel infusions with evidence of clinically relevant GI toxicity at MD Anderson, defined as prolonged or severe diarrhea, nausea or vomiting 28 days or more after CAR-T cell therapy and in whom an upper or lower endoscopy was performed (Extended Data Fig. 1a contains an overview of the entire patient population).

Because the cilta-cel binding region contains two camelid heavy-chain variable domains, CAR+ T cells are detectable by anti-CAMELID staining. We applied anti-CAMELID staining and seqIF imaging (Lunaphore COMET20) to GI biopsies from all 17 patients, analyzing 4,451,929 cells (Extended Data Fig. 1b–e and Methods).

Nine of the 17 patients with enterocolitis demonstrated dense CAR+ infiltrates, operationally defined as ≥20% of the CD3+ T cell population in at least one biopsy site by automated cell counting (Fig. 1a,b, Extended Data Fig. 1f and Supplementary Table 1). The remaining patients with CAR− post-cilta-cel enterocolitis had scattered CAR+ T cells identified comprising <10% of the CD3+ T cell population and <1% of the total cell population (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 2a). When comparing clinical outcomes of post-cilta-cel patients with enterocolitis, we found that patients with ≥20% CAR+ T cell infiltrate had substantially worse clinical courses, requiring a median of 48 hospital days compared to 5 hospital days for the CAR− population (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 2). Patients with CAR+ enterocolitis averaged 2.4 post-endoscopy infections compared to an average of 0.16 in the CAR− group (Extended Data Fig. 2b). Mortality in the CAR+ population was four of nine patients compared to zero of eight CAR− patients, bringing the absolute risk difference for mortality to 44.4% (confidence interval (CI) 5.6–78.4%). Similarly, four of nine patients with CAR+ enterocolitis required total parenteral nutrition (TPN) during their treatment course as compared to zero of eight patients with CAR− enterocolitis (Supplementary Table 2).

a, Multiparameter sequential immunofluorescent imaging of duodenum samples from post-cilta-cel patients with enterocolitis showed that nine patients had dense CAR+ (that is, CAMELID+ marking cilta-cel) infiltrates, which were defined as at least 20% of the CD3+ population in a single biopsy. Anti-CAMELID staining is depicted in scarlet, and pan-cytokeratin (PANK) staining is depicted in white to visualize epithelial cells. IEC-EC cases typically consist of dense CAR+ infiltrations, often in a periglandular distribution. b, Differential CAR+ T cell infiltration by GI site in untreated controls, patients with post-cilta-cel enterocolitis without CAR+ infiltration (CAR−group) and patients with post-cilta-cel IEC-EC as defined by dense CAR+ infiltration, ≥20% of CD3+ cells in at least one biopsy (CAR+ group). Patients with IEC-EC have a median of four biopsies per patient across different GI sites. There is almost no background CAR staining in untreated controls. Some patients with post-cilta-cel EC without IEC-EC have shown small amounts of CAR staining that is typically <5% of CD3+ cells. c, Total hospital days for patients with EC-NOS without CAR+ infiltrate (n = 8) and IEC-EC patients with CAR+ infiltrate (n = 9). Patients with CAR+ IEC-EC spent a median of 48 days in the hospital relative to a median of 5 days for the patients with CAR− EC-NOS (P = 0.0046, two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test without adjustment). One CAR+ patient had a short hospitalization due to presenting in cardiac arrest. The CAR− group included one patient with a diagnosed CAR+ PTCL who also presented with diarrhea. Other CAR− patients were determined to have diarrhea/enterocolitis due to multiple sources, which typically resolved with standard treatments. d, Swimmer plot showing the clinical course of IEC-EC for each patient, ordered by increasing duration of follow-up. Embedded colored boxes indicate individual treatments administered during the clinical course, with cyclophosphamide highlighted in red and cyclosporine in gold. Presenting infections are shown as symbols at the time of infection onset. Black vertical ticks indicate endoscopy timepoints, and open purple circles indicate scRNA-seq peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) sampling timepoints. Red crosses indicate death, and yellow triangles indicate tumor progression. CMV, cytomegalovirus; OR, odds ratio.

We therefore defined IEC-EC as post-cilta-cel enterocolitis with CAR+ cells comprising at least 20% of CD3+ T cells in one GI biopsy. CAR positivity among CD3+ cells varied less by tissue than positivity among all cells, and a 10% threshold selected the same patients (Extended Data Fig. 2c–e). Infiltration was dichotomous in this cohort, typically over multiple biopsies, but subtler cases may emerge. Additionally, automated single-cell quantification is not routinely feasible for clinical diagnosis. Enterocolitis without dense CAR+ infiltration was classified as enterocolitis not otherwise specified (EC-NOS) and served as the control group.

Clinical course and treatment of post-cilta-cel IEC-EC

Baseline clinical characteristics of IEC-EC cases are included in Extended Data Table 1. Clinical courses are detailed in Fig. 1d, Supplementary Tables 1–5, Supplementary Figs. 1–4 and Methods. Seven patients presented primarily with diarrhea, reaching 13 liters per day, and two with nausea or abdominal pain. Median onset was day 61 after infusion (range, 30–541). Seven had infections before or concurrent with IEC-EC. Cyclophosphamide or cyclosporine produced remission or improvement in four patients, whereas primary ruxolitinib and oral steroids generally failed. One patient improved with mesalamine alone, and infliximab improved symptoms without clearing the CAR+ infiltration.

The duodenum is the primary site of IEC-EC CAR+ infiltration

Generalized linear mixed models of SeqIF21 data using estimated marginal means (EMMs) showed greatest CAR+ infiltration in the duodenum of patients with IEC-EC: estimated fractions among CD3+ cells were 63.5% in duodenum, 36.4% in terminal ileum, 14.0% in colon, 6.22% in stomach, 3.36% in rectum and 2.11% in esophagus (Fig. 2a). Thus, IEC-EC is a pan-enterocolitis with predominant small-intestinal, especially duodenal, involvement.

a, CAR+ infiltration in IEC-EC by tissue (n = 1 esophagus, n = 4 stomach, n = 9 duodenum, n = 5 terminal ileum, n = 15 colon, n = 2 rectum). A statistically significant increase in CAR+ infiltration was specifically seen in the duodenum relative to other biopsy sites, followed by the terminal ileum and then the colon. GLMM, P = 2 × 10−8, duodenum versus other tissue OR for CAR+ cells was 9.41 (CI 4.3–20.58). For box plots, the center line indicates the median, boxes span the interquartile range (25th–75th percentiles), and whiskers extend to the most extreme observations within 1.5× the interquartile range below or above the box. GLMM comparisons performed with a two-sided Wald z-test from a beta-binomial generalized linear mixed model without adjustment. b, CD4/CD8 ratio of CAR+ T cells by GI biopsy site. There is a preponderance of CD4+ CAR+ infiltrates, but some biopsies demonstrate preferential CD8+ expression, indicating a high degree of case-by-case variation in T cell lineage. c, Similar comparison of CAR+ cells in n = 36 GI tissue samples relative to adjacent CAR− T cells. CAR+ cells possess increased PD1 and GZMB expression consistent with exhausted cell phenotypes. OR for gain of PD1 in CAR+ cells 4.52 (CI 3.19–6.41), P = 2.87 × 10−17; OR for gain of GZMB in CAR+ cells 2.27 (CI 1.46–3.52); q = 2.69 × 10−4. There is no difference in fractional expression of Ki-67 in CAR+ populations relative to adjacent CAR− T cells. GLMM comparisons used two-sided Wald z-tests from beta-binomial GLMMs without adjustment. d, There is a loss of CD103+ tissue-resident T cells in the GI tissue of IEC-EC relative to EC-NOS, indicating disruption of the normal GI architecture associated with the pathology. OR for differential CD103 expression in CAR+ IEC-EC patients versus no IEC-EC controls is 0.42 (CI 0.26–0.66), P = 2.16 × 10−; GLMM comparisons used two-sided Wald z-tests from beta-binomial GLMMs without adjustment. e, Relation of CAR+ infiltration to CD103+ T cell expression. CD103 indicates TRM T cells that typically occupy gut tissue. There is a negative correlation between CAR+ infiltration in the GI tissue and the presence of CD103+ T cells, suggesting that CAR+ infiltration disrupts the normal T cell architecture of the gut. Two-sided Spearman correlation, ρ = −0.51, P = 0.0015, n = 36 pairs. Shaded area represents 95% CI. CD103, integrin αE; NS, not significant; TRM, tissue-resident memory.

CAR+ T cell infiltrates demonstrate aberrant CD4/CD8 expression

Direct analysis of the CD4/CD8 ratio of CAR+ cells confirmed the presence of both lineages with variable CD4 or CD8 predominance (Fig. 2b). More patients exhibited CD4− predominant infiltrates than CD8− predominant infiltrates, paralleling reports of CD4+CAR+ T cells as a driver for post-cilta-cel toxicity22. However, overall CD4/CD8 ratios were variable, and one patient was predominantly double negative (DN; CD4−CD8−).

For each biopsy, we modeled the fraction of CD3+ cells falling into CD4+, CD8+, double positive (DP; CD4+CD8+) or DN compartments in CAR+ and adjacent CAR⁻ T cells using generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs). No statistically significant differences were observed in CD4+ or CD8+ T cell populations between the groups, likely in part driven by variable CD4/CD8 predominance in the CAR+ infiltrate. However, CAR+ populations were enriched for DP expression and had reduced DN expression (Extended Data Fig. 3a). This result is consistent with a more differentiated, cytotoxic, checkpoint-enriched phenotypic state of CAR+ T cells in the GI tract than adjacent CAR− T cells23,24.

CAR+ T cell infiltrates have an exhausted cytotoxic phenotype and are associated with loss of resident GI CD103+ T cells

We next analyzed programmed cell death protein 1 (PD1), granzyme B (GZMB) and Ki-67 expression in patients with IEC-EC. Ki-67-positivity did not differ between compartments (Fig. 2c). PD1 positivity was higher in CAR+ T cells (51.6%) relative to adjacent CAR− T cells (17.9%). Similarly, GZMB positivity was higher in CAR+ T cells (37.3%) than adjacent CAR− T cells (20.8%) within IEC‑EC biopsies. When comparing post-cilta-cel enterocolitis samples with CAR+ infiltration (IEC‑EC) to those without (EC-NOS), the fraction of GZMB+ T cells was also higher in IEC‑EC versus EC-NOS cohorts. This difference was most pronounced in the duodenum, where the EMMs of GZMB+ T cells were 62.1% in IEC‑EC patients versus 15.2% in EC-NOS (Extended Data Fig. 3b).

We additionally observed a clear depletion of CD103+ tissue-resident memory T cells in IEC‑EC patients. The model‑based fraction of CD103+ cells among the CD3+ T cell population was 18.6% in IEC‑EC versus 35.3% in EC-NOS (Fig. 2d). Within the CAR+ IEC‑EC biopsies, the degree of CD103+ cell depletion correlated inversely with the extent of CAR+ infiltration (Fig. 2e). CAR+ T cells in IEC-EC therefore show a GZMB+PD1+ phenotype and are associated with local displacement of CD103+ T cells.
